name: DOE Paducah AI Campus
heading: 3. DOE Paducah AI Campus — 1,800 MW Planned Utility Service
brief: The U.S. Department of Energy announced on July 29, 2026 that Brookfield , NextEra Energy , and three regional power organizations would pursue an AI and high-performance computing campus on land at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant . The estimated private-sector program exceeds $100 billion , although that figure describes the proposed long-term infrastructure investment, not money already spent. The federal site retains transmission, water, roads, and other infrastructure from its uranium-enrichment history, while environmental cleanup continues. NextEra’s original coalition announcement specifies up to 1.8 GW of utility capacity and more than 1.2 GW of compute capacity at full development, targeted for 2032 . The distinction is important: 1.8 GW measures overall planned electric service, whereas compute capacity is the proposed allocation to IT equipment. The project remains subject to definitive negotiations, utility regulatory oversight, construction approvals, and delivery of new infrastructure. The company gives an initial phase near 155 MW , rising toward 2,000 MW of total campus power . Rubix estimates that full campus power could support roughly 1,400 MW of IT load ; it proposes $8 billion to $12 billion in construction investment before the additional cost of GPUs and other computing hardware. These remain developer assumptions. The Kentucky Lantern’s July 22 reporting connects the proposal to the city’s published questionnaire and the local debate over an earlier data center moratorium. name: ONE Nuclear Project Barracuda
heading: 2. ONE Nuclear Project Barracuda — Up to 1,000 MW Proposed IT Capacity
brief: Project Barracuda entered Louisiana’s data center pipeline in September. In a September 10, 2026 company announcement that was also filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission , ONE Nuclear Energy described a proposed 1.2 GW Energy Park and Technology Campus , with up to approximately 1 GW of critical IT data center capacity . That is the ranking figure. It is a planning-level concept , not a signed tenant lease or commissioned server load. The developer’s preliminary configuration includes approximately 1.2 GW of dispatchable natural-gas generation and 300 MW / 1.2 GWh of battery storage . These figures measure the supply-side infrastructure ; they must not be added to the one-gigawatt planned IT demand. A 300 MW battery output rating describes possible discharge power, while 1.2 GWh describes stored energy and, at rated discharge, corresponds to a nominal four-hour duration. heading: 1. Meta Hyperion, Richland Parish — 5,000 MW Planned Compute Capacity
brief: Meta Hyperion , near Holly Ridge in Richland Parish , is Louisiana’s largest documented AI campus. In its July 13, 2026 update , Meta announced an expansion of its ongoing Richland Parish project to five gigawatts of compute capacity . The expanded long-term investment exceeds $50 billion , and the site is intended to house Meta’s largest multi-gigawatt AI training cluster. The earlier 2024 announcement was substantially smaller; the revised 5 GW scope should not be presented as additional separate campus capacity. The company expects more than 7,500 construction workers at peak and approximately 1,000 positions when fully operational . Meta reports more than $1.6 billion contracted with Louisiana suppliers and additional community investments, including local infrastructure and workforce programs. Its July community announcement describes teacher bonuses and local business growth associated with the project. name: Nautilus, Great Northern Paper Mill, Millinocket
heading: 3. Nautilus, Great Northern Paper Mill, Millinocket — 60 MW Canceled Project
brief: Nautilus Data Technologies had planned a 60 MW data center at the former Great Northern Paper industrial site in Millinocket , with an initial investment proposal around $300 million . Announced in 2021, the development was originally expected to open by the end of 2022 and drew attention for its potential reuse of hydropower-adjacent paper-mill infrastructure. By April 9, 2025 , however, the site’s redevelopment managers confirmed to the Bangor Daily News that the entire project had been canceled. Data Center Dynamics reported the same status on April 16. The company reportedly struggled to secure a suitable AI tenant and sufficient power for the anticipated workload. Steve Sanders, director of mill redevelopment at One Katahdin, said the project was abandoned. Therefore the 60 MW remains an earlier proposal, not current capacity . The site has continued to pursue other kinds of industrial reuse. In any 2026 operating-load comparison, the canceled Nautilus plan contributes zero commissioned data center megawatts ; it appears in this historical proposal ranking only to document Maine

name: Sentinel / JGT2, Androscoggin Mill, Jay
heading: 2. Sentinel / JGT2, Androscoggin Mill, Jay — 82 MW Existing Utility Allotment; Project on Hold
brief: At the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay, Franklin County , property owner JGT2 Redevelopment and intended data-center operator Sentinel Data Centers had proposed converting industrial buildings into a roughly $550 million computing campus. The mill already held a Central Maine Power agreement for 82 MW of electric service. In an May 4, 2026 developer interview , JGT2 principal Tony McDonald said the data center might initially use around 50–55 MW and could grow toward the 82 MW utility allotment. That makes 82 MW a service ceiling or availability reference , rather than a measured or formally designed critical IT load. Another source distinguishes the planned grid import even more sharply. Public-record tracking reports that developers expected to draw up to 25 MW from Central Maine Power under their proposed combination of existing hydro and future solar supply. The same record identifies up to 150 MW of solar generation as a separate concept. name: Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center, Holyoke
heading: 3. Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center, Holyoke — Up to 12 MW Permitted Grid Draw
brief: The Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center is an established nonprofit scientific computing facility used by researchers at Harvard, MIT, the University of Massachusetts, Northeastern, Boston University and Yale. Unlike the two larger proposals, this facility is operating. WBUR reported September 11, 2026 that MGHPCC is permitted to draw up to 12 MW from the electricity grid and was using less than its maximum allowance. The 12 MW is a grid-draw permit ceiling , not a claimed measurement of current servers or IT load. The Holyoke center was exempted from the city’s new-data-center restrictions. Its existing building demonstrates how hydropower-heavy local electricity, outside-air cooling and carefully managed server temperatures can support academic workloads. A 12 MW draw maintained for 24 hours would correspond to 288 MWh , but that is an illustrative maximum-rate calculation rather than observed daily consumption. Its actual operating draw was reported below the permit ceiling.

name: Chestnut River Power, Holyoke
heading: 2. Chestnut River Power, Holyoke — 20 MW Proposed; Stalled
brief: A separate 20 MW data center proposal at 100 Water Street by Chestnut River Power and Infrastructure prompted debate about new AI computing facilities in Holyoke. On June 16, 2026 , the City Council voted 9–4 for a zoning restriction on new AI data centers above 12 MW, exempting the existing MGHPCC. The developer subsequently said it was reviewing the city’s decision rather than announcing an operational facility. The Hampden County project record tracks the proposal as stalled. A October 27, 2026 city-council report confirms Holyoke is still studying future policy and potential economic, power and water impacts. The 20 MW figure is the proposed new center’s power scale , not an existing grid connection or commissioned computing capacity. The city’s June ordinance must not be confused with a statewide Massachusetts ban, and MGHPCC’s exemption does not authorize the proposed new site.
